title: Missing Data & Types
blurb: Missing values are data about the data: decide per column what absence means, then fill or drop with intent.

cells.title: NaN is a number — and that changes your column
cells.body:
In pandas, a missing value in a numeric column is stored as NaN, which is a float. The moment one reading is missing, the whole column becomes float64 — your integer counts silently turn into 3.0. That is why .isna() (a mask of where values are missing) and .notna() are the first tools to reach for: they let you see absence as data before deciding what to do about it.

Row semantics decides the treatment. A missing qty in an inventory row often means "zero were counted", while a missing answer in a survey row often means "no answer" — a row that maybe should not count at all. Same NaN, opposite meanings, different operations. Neither is a syntax choice; it is a claim about the world the table describes.

demo.code:
import pandas as pd

stock = pd.DataFrame({
    "item": ["bolt", "nut", "washer"],
    "qty": [100, None, 12],
})
print(stock.dtypes.to_dict())
print(stock["qty"].isna().tolist())
print(stock["qty"].fillna(0).tolist())

cells.title: Fill vs drop: two families, two questions
cells.body:
fillna answers "what should I pretend the missing value was?" — a constant like 0, or something derived like the column mean. dropna answers "which rows are too incomplete to use?" — and its thresh parameter is the precise way to express it: dropna(subset=questions, thresh=3) keeps only rows with at least 3 non-missing values among the question columns.

Notice both are still row questions. fillna changes cells per column; dropna removes whole rows. Choosing between them is not a syntax decision — it is a decision about what a half-empty row means in your scenario, and the counting version (notna().sum(axis=1)) makes the "how complete is this row?" question inspectable before you commit to a rule.

demo.code:
import pandas as pd

survey = pd.DataFrame({
    "person": ["ana", "bo", "cy"],
    "q1": [5, None, 3],
    "q2": [4, 2, None],
    "q3": [None, None, 1],
})
answered = survey[["q1", "q2", "q3"]].notna().sum(axis=1)
print(answered.tolist())
print(survey.dropna(subset=["q1", "q2", "q3"], thresh=2))

cells.title: Dirty text columns: coerce first, then decide
cells.body:
Real exports arrive with "1,250", " 42 ", "n/a" and blanks all mixed into one column. pd.to_numeric(s, errors="coerce") converts what it can and turns the rest into NaN — a single, inspectable place where all the junk lands. After coercing you can decide with full information: drop those rows, count them, or treat them as zero.

The coercion-first habit matters because it separates parsing from policy. Parsing is mechanical — strip spaces, remove thousands separators, coerce. Policy — what a failed parse means for the total — depends on what the rows represent. When a solution mixes the two, every new junk format breaks the logic; when they are separate, new junk just falls into the NaN bucket you already handle.

demo.code:
import pandas as pd

raw = pd.Series(["1,250", " 42 ", "n/a", 7.5])
text = raw.astype(str).str.strip().str.replace(",", "")
clean = pd.to_numeric(text, errors="coerce")
print(clean.tolist())
print("unparseable:", clean.isna().sum())

exercise.title: Fill the gaps in inventory
exercise.statement:
A store keeps a stock table. Each row is one product with columns item (str), qty (count, may be missing) and price (may be missing).

A missing qty means nobody counted that shelf — the shop treats it as 0. A missing price means the price was never entered — the shop fills those with the default price 9.99.

Implement fill_defaults(stock) returning a DataFrame with the same columns ["item", "qty", "price"] in the same row order, where every missing qty is replaced by 0 and every missing price by 9.99. The returned frame contains no missing values.
constraints: Same columns ['item', 'qty', 'price'] in that order, same rows in the same order
Missing qty becomes 0; missing price becomes 9.99
The returned DataFrame has no missing values anywhere

examples.call: fill_defaults(stock)  # rows: bolt 100 @ 0.15, nut missing @ 0.05, washer 12 @ missing
examples.returns: DataFrame with columns ['item', 'qty', 'price']: bolt 100 @ 0.15, nut 0 @ 0.05, washer 12 @ 9.99
examples.why: the uncounted shelf becomes qty 0 and the unentered price becomes the default 9.99; recorded values stay untouched
fillna only touches missing cells, so a complete table passes through as-is

exercise.starter:
import pandas as pd

def fill_defaults(stock):
    """Return stock with missing qty filled by 0 and missing
    price filled by 9.99.

    Same columns, same row order, no missing values left.
    """
    pass
hints: What does a missing value in the qty column mean here, and what number stands for that meaning? And for price?
One fillna call can take a dictionary mapping each column name to its own fill value — no need to fill the two columns separately.
return stock.fillna({'qty': 0, 'price': 9.99}) — the dict form applies a per-column constant and leaves present values alone.
exercise.reasoning: Imputation is where row semantics becomes visible: a missing qty and a missing price are both NaN, but they are filled with different constants, because absence means different things in the two columns. The dictionary form of fillna exists precisely for this — it encodes "what absence means" as data, one entry per column. Also note what fillna promises not to do: it never touches cells that already hold values, so a complete table passes through unchanged, which is exactly the contract the tests rely on.

exercise.title: Keep the serious respondents
exercise.statement:
A survey tool exported one row per person. Each row of survey has columns respondent (str, never missing) and q1, q2, q3, q4 (answers; each may be missing).

The analysis should only use serious respondents: people who answered at least min_answers of the four questions (a non-missing q1..q4 counts as an answer).

Implement serious_respondents(survey, min_answers) returning a Series named respondent listing, in the same order as the table, the respondents who answered at least min_answers questions.
constraints: A respondent counts as serious when at least min_answers of q1..q4 are non-missing
min_answers may be 0 (everyone qualifies) or larger than 4 (nobody does)
Return a Series named 'respondent' with the qualifying names in original table order
The respondent column itself is never missing

examples.call: serious_respondents(survey, 3)  # ana answered 3, bo answered 1, cy answered 3
examples.why: ana and cy each have 3 non-missing answers, which meets the 'at least 3' bar; bo's single answer does not
with the bar at 1, everyone who answered anything qualifies, and everyone did

exercise.starter:
import pandas as pd

def serious_respondents(survey, min_answers):
    """Return the names of respondents who answered at least
    min_answers of the four questions.

    Series named 'respondent', original table order.
    """
    pass

tests.label: bar of four needs all answers
bar of zero includes empty answers

hints: "At least k of the four questions" is a property of a whole row, not of any single cell. How could you count, per row, how many of q1..q4 are present?
notna() gives a True/False frame; summing across axis=1 turns each row into a count of answered questions. Compare that count to min_answers and index the respondent column with the mask.

answered = survey[['q1','q2','q3','q4']].notna().sum(axis=1); return survey.loc[answered >= min_answers, 'respondent'].reset_index(drop=True). (dropna(subset=[...], thresh=min_answers) does the same row-keeping.)
exercise.reasoning: The reframe: "serious respondent" is a row-level property — a count of present cells among four specific columns — and pandas lets you compute that count per row with notna().sum(axis=1). Once completeness is a column of integers, the filter is an ordinary comparison. This is the reasoning behind dropna(thresh=...) too: thresh is exactly "keep rows with at least this many non-missing values in the subset". The order guarantee comes free, because both approaches are boolean row selection, which never reorders.

exercise.title: Total the messy ledger
exercise.statement:
An accounting export was supposed to have one number per row, but the amount column of ledger (columns: entry str, amount) is a mess: real numbers mixed with strings like "1250.5", "1,250.50" (thousands separator), " 42 " (surrounding spaces), and unparseable junk like "n/a" or "?".

Implement ledger_total(ledger) that:

  • cleans: treats each cell as text, strips surrounding spaces and removes commas, so "1,250.50" reads 1250.50;
  • coerces: converts with pd.to_numeric(..., errors="coerce") — cells that still fail contribute nothing;
  • aggregates: returns the total of all parseable amounts as a single float rounded to 2 decimal places (0 if nothing parses).
constraints: Cleaning = treat the cell as text (astype(str)), strip whitespace, remove commas — nothing else
Unparseable cells (after cleaning) contribute 0 to the total
Return a single float rounded to 2 decimal places; 0.0 when nothing parses
Numbers stored as ints or floats must still count, e.g. the value 7.5 in a string column

examples.why: 1250.5 + 1250.50 + 42 + 7.25 parse and sum; 'n/a' coerces to missing and contributes nothing
the bare int and the string '20' both parse; '?' does not

exercise.starter:
import pandas as pd

def ledger_total(ledger):
    """Return the total of the parseable amounts, rounded to
    2 decimal places.

    Clean each cell as text (strip spaces, drop commas), then
    coerce with errors='coerce'; unparseable cells add nothing.
    """
    pass
hints: Why does .str.strip() crash or lose data on a column that mixes numbers and strings? What single conversion makes every cell a string first?
Three steps in order: text = ledger['amount'].astype(str).str.strip().str.replace(',', '') — then amounts = pd.to_numeric(text, errors='coerce') — then a sum that skips the NaNs.

amounts = pd.to_numeric(ledger['amount'].astype(str).str.strip().str.replace(',', ''), errors='coerce'); return round(float(amounts.sum()), 2). Series.sum() skips missing values by default, so junk adds nothing.
exercise.reasoning: This pipeline is parse, then policy. Parsing is mechanical: astype(str) normalizes the mixed-type column (real numbers become their text form, so 7.5 survives the trip), strip and comma-removal undo cosmetic damage, and errors="coerce" quarantines everything still unreadable into NaN. Policy is one decision at the end — unparseable entries contribute nothing — expressed by the fact that .sum() skips missing values. Because the junk decision is a single, explicit step, new junk formats land in the same NaN bucket instead of crashing a hand-rolled parser, and the final round(., 2) keeps float noise out of the ledger.
